title: Self-Portrait Photography: How to Photograph Yourself Alone — cv.cm
description: How to take self-portraits with no photographer: tripod setup, timer, interval and burst, phone remotes, focusing on a stand-in, framing marks and a workflow.
h1: How do you take good photos of yourself without a photographer?
answer: Put the camera or phone on a tripod at chest height, frame the scene with extra space, and mark your spot on the ground. Focus with face detection or on a stand-in object at your mark, use f/4 to f/5.6 for a safety margin, and trigger with a phone app, a remote, or a 10-second timer with several shots per press.

body: A selfie is taken at arm's length, usually with the front camera. A self-portrait uses a camera placed somewhere else, so the photo looks as if another person took it: full-length shots, wide scenes, a longer lens, and the better rear camera of a phone. This guide is for the second kind. For arm's-length photos, see the selfie tips guide on this shelf.
The main problems when you shoot yourself are three: you cannot see the frame while posing, focus must land where you will be, and you must press the shutter from far away. Each has a simple fix.

body: Do not balance a camera on something that can tip, such as a railing over water or a car roof. Tripods in some parks, museums and landmarks need permission; check the rules and keep paths clear.

ul: Self-timer: every camera and phone has one. On most phones you can choose 3 or 10 seconds; on cameras, 2, 5, 10 or 20 seconds. Use 10 seconds to walk to your spot.
Timer with several frames: many cameras let you set the timer to take 3 to 10 frames per press. Some phones take a short burst with the timer. You get several expressions for each walk.
Interval shooting (intervalometer): the camera takes a photo every few seconds, for example every 3 seconds for 5 minutes. You move freely and choose later. Check the card space.
Phone app remote: camera makers such as Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm and OM System have free apps that show the live view on your phone and fire the shutter. You can check the framing from your spot.
Bluetooth remote: a small button that works with many phones and some cameras, easy to hide in a hand or behind a bouquet.
Infrared remote: needs a clear line from the remote to the camera's sensor, usually in front of the camera, and works only a few meters away.
Hands-free phone features: some phones can start the timer when you raise your palm, or take a photo on a voice command. A smartwatch can often act as a remote with a live view.

body: For video-style portraits, some people record 4K video and take frames from it. The quality is lower than a still photo, and the shutter speed of video often blurs movement.

sections.h: Focusing when you are not there
body: Focus is the most common failure in self-portraits: the background is sharp and the face is soft, because the camera focused on whatever was there when you pressed the button.

ol: Face or eye detection: on most recent cameras and phones, the camera finds your face when you arrive. Set the focus mode to continuous (AF-C) with face detection, and use the timer or app so it has time to lock.

Stand-in method: put an object on your mark at head height (a bag on a chair, a jacket on a light stand). Focus on it, then switch the lens or camera to manual focus (MF) so the focus does not change. Remove the object and stand in its place.
Phone lock: tap your mark and hold until the phone shows a focus and exposure lock (on iPhone, AE/AF Lock). Then walk into the frame. If you stand somewhere else, focus will be wrong.
Depth of field as a safety margin: close the aperture a little so small errors still look sharp.

body: These figures use the common 0.03 mm circle of confusion. For a sharp face with some background blur, a good starting point is a 50 mm lens at f/4 from about 3 m. Phone main cameras have small sensors and keep a lot in focus, so focus is less critical; portrait mode adds blur afterwards.

ol: Choose the light first. Face a window, stand in open shade, or shoot in the last hour before sunset with the sun to one side.
Set the tripod. Chest height for half-body shots; waist height for full-length shots so the legs do not look short.
Frame with extra space around where you will stand. You can crop later; you cannot add space.
Mark your spot with a small object, and decide where your feet go.

Set exposure: aperture priority, f/4 to f/5.6, ISO auto with a limit around 1600, shutter 1/250 s or faster if you will move. On a phone, lock exposure on your mark and lower it slightly if the scene is very bright.
Set focus with face detection, the stand-in method or the phone lock.
Fire with the app, a remote, or the timer with several frames.
Check: after the first set, walk back and zoom in on your eyes. Check the edges of the frame and the background for poles or signs behind your head.
Change one thing per round: pose, angle, facing direction, expression. Then repeat.
Keep notes: if a framing works, take a phone photo of the tripod position to find it again next time.

body: Posing alone is easier with movement. Walk into the frame during the timer, turn, look back, adjust your clothes. Use the poses in the how-to-pose guide on this shelf, and see cv.cm's pose reference for standing, sitting and looking-back positions. To practise aperture and distance choices without leaving home, cv.cm's portrait camera simulator shows how blur changes with lens, aperture and subject distance.

ul: Window portrait: sit beside a window, side light, a plain wall behind you.
Hands only or back only: if you do not want to show your face, photograph your hands with a book or cup, or your back looking at a view.
Walking in a scene: tripod low on a path, walk past with a 10-second interval running.
Outfit or style record: same spot, same framing, different outfits; a set looks good as a grid.
Milestone portraits: a birthday, a graduation, a solo bridal session in a dress or suit.
Silhouette: stand in front of a bright window or sunset and expose for the bright area.

faq.q: How do I take pictures of myself without a tripod?
faq.a: Rest the camera or phone on a stable surface such as a wall, a table or a stack of books, wedged so it cannot slide. Use the timer and check the first frame before posing more.

faq.q: How do I take a full-body photo of myself with my phone?
faq.a: Put the phone at waist height on a tripod or shelf, use the 1x rear camera from about 2 to 3 m, lock focus on your spot, and use a 10-second timer or a Bluetooth remote.

faq.q: How do I keep focus when taking self-portraits?
faq.a: Use face or eye detection, or focus on an object placed exactly where you will stand and then switch to manual focus. A slightly smaller aperture such as f/4 to f/5.6 adds a safety margin.

faq.q: Can I control my camera with my phone?
faq.a: Many cameras from Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm and OM System work with the maker's free phone app, which shows the live view and fires the shutter. Check your camera manual for remote shooting support.

faq.q: What is the best timer setting for self-portraits?
faq.a: Ten seconds, with several frames per press if your camera offers it. For moving shots, interval shooting every 2 to 3 seconds gives more choice.
